title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes the verifier-detected safety-violation rate of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N=500 intent→configuration tasks) we compared (1) baseline: a single LLM proposal (gpt-5-mini) and (2) guarded: the same LLM proposal screened by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); absolute paired success-rate difference = 0.002; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006]. Crucially, the design used a single shared initial generation per task (shared_initial_candidate) that was evaluated under both arms; model-call accounting therefore equals one initial generation per task plus any repair-stage calls (model_calls_used = 501; repair calls = 1). On this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and this model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals, so the marginal measured verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric was numerically small. We archive the preregistration, execution manifest, prompts, outputs, and validator traces and clarify execution-accounting and interpretive limits required for correct reading of the result.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and limited self-healing. Prior system and survey work emphasizes that operational reliability depends on both model capability and surrounding engineering (validators, sandboxing, canarying, rollback) rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate→verify→repair patterns (verify-in-the-loop) are commonly proposed to improve correctness of structured outputs, but controlled measurements that isolate the verifier contribution are scarce. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer a focused question: how much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals, compared to LLM-only proposals, when tasks and topologies are canonical and restricted to verifier-modeled features? The paper reports the preregistered design, execution, and confirmatory analysis and clarifies execution accounting and verifier scope required for correct interpretation.
sections.related_work: Deterministic and formal network-verification methods (header-space analyses, route-model verifiers) can check reachability, isolation, and other properties on configuration models and have been used to reason about updates and safety [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps work integrates LLMs into intent-driven pipelines and emphasizes that validators and operational guardrails are essential for safe automation [Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair loops and verifier-assisted self-correction have been studied in code and configuration domains; however, public controlled ablations that quantify verifier effect size in LLM-driven NetOps pipelines are limited. Failure-mode studies of LLM applications motivate guardrails: hallucination, overconfidence, and tool/encoding failures can produce hazardous operational recommendations absent validation [Owen, 2026]. Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact-backed paired measurement isolating verifier+repair impact under constrained synthetic conditions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The experiment was preregistered before execution (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026; preregistration artifact archived—preregistration SHA-256 starts 405a9f882cbf...—see execution manifest). Confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus one automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task comparison). Sampling and tasks: 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks were generated deterministically and stratified across canonical clusters (VLAN-change, ACL-change, static-route-change) per the preregistration sampling plan; tasks referencing features not modeled by the verifier were to be excluded from the primary analysis (no such exclusions occurred). Model and orchestration: LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Shared-generation semantics and model-call accounting (required clarification): the preregistered transformation used generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' and independent_condition_generation = false: for each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal which served as the baseline output and was also evaluated by the guarded arm. The guarded arm invoked an automated repair iteration only if the validator reported preregistered high/medium-severity violations on that shared candidate. This isolates verifier+repair impact conditional on the same initial candidate rather than measuring verifier-guided regeneration. Execution-accounting artifacts that define these semantics are archived in the evidence bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json in the artifact bundle). Analysis plan: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar two-sided (alpha = 0.05); paired-bootstrap for 95% CI (B = 10000, seed = 1729). Missingness, exclusions, and retries followed the preregistration policy; analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1.
sections.results: Execution summary (artifact-backed): completed pairs = 500; model_calls_used = 501. Provider-audit stage_counts record a single shared_initial_generation stage with 500 provider calls and a repair stage with 1 provider call; deterministic reconciliation in the manifest confirms these counts. Mapping of counts to outcomes (required reconciliation): because a single shared initial LLM proposal was generated per task, baseline outcomes were derived from the shared candidate without additional model calls. The guarded arm re-used the shared candidate for its validator evaluation and invoked the repair-stage provider call only for the single task where the validator reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Hence model_calls_used = 500 (initial shared generations) + 1 (repair-stage call) = 501. The manifest's condition_counts keys (e.g., {shared:500, guarded:1}) reflect provider-call accounting across stages (shared_initial_generation vs repair) and do not count per-task guarded evaluations; guarded_success_count = 500 counts tasks whose final validated configuration passed, not the number of repair-stage calls. Confirmatory outcomes (analysis/ results): baseline_success_count = 499 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded_success_count = 500 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0020000000000000018. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Repair activity and exclusions: zero tasks were excluded from primary analysis for unmodeled features; repair-stage provider calls observed = 1. Statistical interpretation (required clarification): the exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 arises because only one discordant pair (n10=1, n01=0) was observed and the majority of pairs were concordant in the pass direction; with such a ceiling effect the two-sided exact permutation calculation yields a large p-value and wide inference uncertainty for small absolute differences. The paired-bootstrap CI quantifies the possible absolute improvement consistent with the data (≤ 0.006).
sections.discussion: On this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and with the tested model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals (499/500 baseline passes), leaving little room for additional verifier+repair improvements on the pass-rate metric. The single discordant task demonstrates that the guarded loop can correct rare baseline failures, confirming verifier value as a formal safety gate. Importantly, measured verifier impact depends on (a) baseline LLM error prevalence on the evaluated distribution and (b) verifier modeling coverage. Because the validator was designed to model the fields used by the synthetic task generator (representative task payloads show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}) and the task corpus avoided unmodeled features, external generalization to production environments with cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity or broader protocol semantics is limited. Operational implication: where baseline proposal error rates are higher or verifier coverage is broader, measured verifier+repair benefit on safety metrics is expected to be larger. Alternative designs (not executed here) that permit verifier-feedback-guided regeneration or larger repair budgets answer different operational questions: they would measure how guidance from verifier failures drives alternative candidate generation rather than conditional repair of a single candidate. Those alternatives remain future work.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) comparing an LLM-only pipeline to an LLM plus deterministic verifier and one automated repair iteration under shared-initial-generation semantics. Both arms achieved near-perfect verifier pass rates (baseline 499/500, guarded 500/500), producing an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00). The result quantifies a ceiling-effect regime in which an already-accurate LLM leaves limited measured marginal utility for a verifier on the pass-rate metric; it does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in broader or noisier operational settings. Practitioners should measure proposal error prevalence and verifier coverage on realistic workloads to prioritize guardrail investments. All preregistration, execution, prompt, output, and validator artifacts are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle for independent verification.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope (representative task payloads show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}).
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies may change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) creates a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the observed non-significant exact McNemar p = 1.00 should be interpreted in that context rather than as evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary.
